claim: AnkR is highly enriched in the perisomatic region of a subset of neurons sparsely distributed throughout the cortex and hippocampus in mice.
source: We found that AnkR is highly enriched in the perisomatic region of a subset of neurons sparsely distributed throughout the cortex and hippocampus (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: AnkR protein in the brain increases during early postnatal development, reaching mature expression levels by postnatal day 30.
source: Immunoblotting of brain homogenates shows AnkR protein in the brain increases during early postnatal development, reaching mature expression levels by postnatal day 30 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: >90% of Pv+ cells in adult cortex and hippocampus have high levels of AnkR.
source: immunostaining with antibodies against parvalbumin (Pv), a marker of fast-spiking interneurons (Figure 1C,D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), shows >90% of Pv+ cells in adult cortex and hippocampus have high levels of AnkR
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 79% of AnkR+ cells in cortex are Pv+.
source: while only 79% of AnkR+ cells in cortex and 64% in hippocampus are Pv+.
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data.

claim: 64% of AnkR+ cells in hippocampus are Pv+.
source: while only 79% of AnkR+ cells in cortex and 64% in hippocampus are Pv+.
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data.

claim: Somatostatin (SST) is expressed in 8% of AnkR+ neurons in cortex.
source: Somatostatin (SST) expressing interneurons account for some of the remaining AnkR+ cells, with SST expressed in 8% of AnkR+ neurons in cortex and 22% of AnkR+ cells in hippocampus (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: Somatostatin (SST) is expressed in 22% of AnkR+ cells in hippocampus.
source: Somatostatin (SST) expressing interneurons account for some of the remaining AnkR+ cells, with SST expressed in 8% of AnkR+ neurons in cortex and 22% of AnkR+ cells in hippocampus (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: AnkR is highly expressed in Pv+ neurons in human brain.
source: AnkR is also highly expressed in Pv+ neurons in human brain.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining of human cortical biopsies shown in Figure 1E.

claim: AnkR staining was identified in laminae II-VI in human cortical biopsy samples.
source: AnkR staining was identified in laminae II-VI in human cortical biopsy samples.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining of human cortical biopsies.

claim: AnkR labeling was strong and membranous and was most intense in larger neurons of laminae III and V in human cortex.
source: Labeling was strong and membranous and was most intense in larger neurons of laminae III and V (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining of human cortical biopsies shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A subset of AnkR+ neurons in laminae III and V co-expressed Pv in the neuronal cytoplasm in human cortex.
source: A subset of AnkR+ neurons in laminae III and V co-expressed Pv in the neuronal cytoplasm (Figure 1E)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining of human cortical biopsies shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The total number of AnkR+ positive neurons exceed the number of Pv+ cells in human cortex.
source: although, as in mice, the total number of AnkR+ positive neurons exceed the number of Pv+ cells.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining of human cortical biopsies.

claim: AnkR and β1 spectrin colocalize in forebrain interneurons.
source: Immunostaining showed that β1 spectrin is highly expressed and colocalizes with AnkR in forebrain interneurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: β1 spectrin and AnkR reciprocally co-immunoprecipitate each other.
source: Furthermore, β1 spectrin and AnkR reciprocally co-immunoprecipitate each other (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: β1 spectrin protein levels are significantly reduced in the absence of AnkR in mouse brain.
source: Immunoblots of Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mouse brain homogenates show that β1 spectrin protein levels are significantly reduced in the absence of AnkR compared to control mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: β1 spectrin immunofluorescence is remarkably reduced in cortex and hippocampus from Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mice compared to control mice.
source: Similarly, immunostaining of cortex and hippocampus from Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mice showed remarkably reduced β1 spectrin immunofluorescence compared to control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: AnkR interacts with and maintains β1 spectrin in forebrain interneurons.
source: Together, these results show that AnkR interacts with and maintains β1 spectrin in forebrain interneurons.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation, immunoblot, and immunostaining data.

claim: TenascinR (TnR) strongly labels AnkR+ neurons in cortex.
source: Immunostaining of cortex revealed that antibodies against TnR and Bcan strongly label AnkR+ neurons (Figure 2E,F)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Brevican (Bcan) strongly labels AnkR+ neurons in cortex.
source: Immunostaining of cortex revealed that antibodies against TnR and Bcan strongly label AnkR+ neurons (Figure 2E,F)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Versican (Vcan) immunoreactivity was not restricted to AnkR+ neurons and was more widely distributed.
source: Vcan immunoreactivity was not restricted to AnkR+ neurons and was more widely distributed (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Aggrecan (Acan) shows strong colocalization with AnkR.
source: Immunostaining for the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan and PNN protein Aggrecan (Acan) (Carulli et al., 2007; Rowlands et al., 2018) also showed strong colocalization with AnkR (Figure 2G)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: AnkR+ neurons are surrounded by WFA-labeled PNNs.
source: Co-staining of WFA and AnkR shows that AnkR+ neurons are surrounded by WFA-labeled PNNs (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: NrCAM shows strong colocalization with both AnkR+ and WFA+ neurons in caudoputamen.
source: Immunostaining for NrCAM showed strong colocalization with both AnkR+ and WFA+ neurons in caudoputamen (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: NrCAM shows less robust colocalization with AnkR+ and WFA+ neurons in hippocampus and cortex.
source: but less robust colocalization in hippocampus and cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Perisomatic NrCAM immunoreactivity was dramatically reduced in Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mouse brain.
source: Perisomatic, but not AIS, NrCAM immunoreactivity was dramatically reduced in Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mouse brain (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: AIS NrCAM immunoreactivity was not reduced in Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mouse brain.
source: Perisomatic, but not AIS, NrCAM immunoreactivity was dramatically reduced in Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mouse brain (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: NrCAM and AnkR reciprocally co-immunoprecipitate each other.
source: Furthermore, NrCAM and AnkR reciprocally co-immunoprecipitate each other (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: PlexinA4 co-immunoprecipitates with AnkR from brain homogenates.
source: Nevertheless, we found that PlexinA4 and Nrp1 co-immunoprecipitated with AnkR from brain homogenates (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Neuropilin-1 (Nrp1) co-immunoprecipitates with AnkR from brain homogenates.
source: Nevertheless, we found that PlexinA4 and Nrp1 co-immunoprecipitated with AnkR from brain homogenates (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Neuropilin-1 (Nrp1) shows strong enrichment in AnkR+ neurons in deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: immunostaining for Nrp1 showed strong enrichment in AnkR+ neurons in deep cerebellar nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: At 1 month of age, there is little difference in the number of WFA+/Pv+, WFA-/Pv+, or WFA+/Pv- neurons per unit area in either hippocampus or cortex between control and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice.
source: At this age, we found little difference in the number of WFA+/Pv+, WFA-/Pv+, or WFA+/Pv- neurons per unit area (UA) in either hippocampus or cortex (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 1 month of age, there is a significant reduction in WFA fluorescence intensity in both cortex and hippocampus in Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice compared to control mice.
source: However, when we measured the fluorescence intensity of WFA, we found a significant reduction in both cortex and hippocampus in Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice compared to floxed or Cre controls (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of AnkR, PNNs are less compact and disrupted compared to control mice at 1 month of age.
source: Examination of PNNs at high magnification showed that in the absence of AnkR, PNNs were less compact and disrupted compared to control mice.
evidence: Supported by high-magnification imaging and semi-quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: AnkR-deficient neurons at 1 month of age are significantly less likely to be compact and more likely to have large holes in their nets.
source: AnkR-deficient neurons were significantly less likely to be compact, characterized as being more likely to have large holes in their nets, and increased WFA thickness (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by semi-quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: AnkR-deficient neurons at 1 month of age have increased WFA thickness.
source: AnkR-deficient neurons were significantly less likely to be compact, characterized as being more likely to have large holes in their nets, and increased WFA thickness (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: In 12-month-old mice, there is a significant reduction in the number of WFA+/Pv+ cells per unit area in the hippocampus and cortex of Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice compared to floxed controls.
source: In 12-month-old mice, we found a significant reduction in the number of WFA+/Pv+ cells per unit area in the hippocampus and cortex of Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice compared to floxed controls (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: In 12-month-old mice, there is a ~50% decrease in the WFA fluorescence intensity in both hippocampus and cortex in Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice.
source: In addition, and like in the one-month-old Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice, we measured a ~50% decrease in the WFA fluorescence intensity in both hippocampus and cortex (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The normally compact PNN structure in 12-month-old control mice is significantly disrupted in Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice with more prominent holes in the PNNs and increased WFA thickness.
source: The normally compact PNN structure, as observed in 12-month-old control mice, was also significantly disrupted in Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice with even more prominent holes in the PNNs, and increased WFA thickness compared to either control or one-month-old Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice (Figure 3J–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by semi-quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3J-L and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The strong reduction in NrCAM immunoreactivity in Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mouse brain is matched by a strong reduction in WFA+ cells in the same region.
source: Furthermore, the strong reduction in NrCAM immunoreactivity seen in Ank1F/F;Nes-Cre mouse brain (Figure 2J) was matched by a strong reduction in WFA+ cells in the same region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Loss of AnkR does not disrupt the ability of PNNs to form, but rather AnkR helps maintain PNNs and their normal compact structure.
source: Together, these results suggest that loss of AnkR does not disrupt the ability of PNNs to form, but rather AnkR helps maintain PNNs and their normal compact structure through binding to PNN-interacting CAMs like NrCAM and PlexinA4.
evidence: Supported by the observation that PNNs still assemble in the absence of AnkR but are less compact and have reduced intensity.

claim: Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice spent significantly more time in the center of the arena and less time in the perimeter compared to both Ank1F/F and Ank1+/+;Dlx5/6-Cre mice during the open-field assessment.
source: Nevertheless, during the open-field assessment, Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice spent significantly more time in the center of the arena and less time in the perimeter compared to both Ank1F/F and Ank1+/+;Dlx5/6-Cre mice (Figure 4B,C)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Loss of AnkR may be anxiolytic.
source: suggesting that loss of AnkR may be anxiolytic.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice spent more time in the center of the open field.

claim: In the elevated plus maze, there is no difference among the three genotypes in the velocity or total distance traveled in all arms.
source: In contrast to the open-field assessment, during a 10-min trial in the elevated plus maze we observed no difference among the three genotypes in the velocity or total distance traveled in all arms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice show a significant increase in the distance traveled in the open arms and the time spent in the open arms in the elevated plus maze compared to control mice.
source: However, we measured a significant increase in the distance traveled in the open arms and the time spent in the open arms by Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice compared to control mice (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Loss of AnkR from forebrain GABAergic neurons reduces anxiety-like behaviors.
source: Together, these data suggest that loss of AnkR from forebrain GABAergic neurons reduces anxiety-like behaviors.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from open field and elevated plus maze assays.

claim: 64 out of 66 WFA+ cells recorded were fast-spiking interneurons.
source: Indeed, 64 out of 66 WFA+ cells recorded were fast-spiking interneurons and the two non-fast spiking cells were not included in the analysis.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The resting membrane potential, input resistance, membrane capacitance, and rheobase current were not significantly altered in Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre neurons compared to controls.
source: We found that the resting membrane potential, input resistance, membrane capacitance, and rheobase current were not significantly altered in Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre neurons compared to controls (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Loss of AnkR decreased the action potential latency and threshold.
source: Loss of AnkR decreased the action potential latency and threshold (Figure 5B,C, and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Loss of AnkR did not change the amplitude of the action potential.
source: without changing the amplitude of the action potential (Figure 5D, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Loss of AnkR altered the shape of the action potential, resulting in a 47% broader action potential with a shallower and delayed AHP.
source: Interestingly, loss of AnkR also altered the shape of the action potential, resulting in a 47% broader action potential with a shallower and delayed AHP (Figure 5E–H, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Loss of AnkR resulted in altered phase plane plots and a reduced maximum dV/dt.
source: Furthermore, loss of AnkR also resulted in altered phase plane plots and a reduced maximum dV/dt (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Loss of AnkR decreased the firing frequency during the first 100 ms of current injection at two times the action potential threshold current.
source: At two times, the action potential threshold current, fast-spiking interneurons from Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice display a decreased firing frequency during the first 100 ms of current injection (Figure 5K)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Loss of AnkR did not change spike frequency adaptation at two times the action potential threshold current.
source: but normal spike frequency adaptation (Figure 5L).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Loss of AnkR enhanced spike amplitude adaptation, resulting in a strong reduction in the amplitudes of action potentials toward the end of spike trains.
source: However, the spike amplitude adaptation was enhanced, resulting in a strong reduction in the amplitudes of action potentials toward the end of spike trains (Figure 5I,M).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5I,M.

claim: Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre cells often entered depolarization block at much lower current levels than control cells.
source: In fact, Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre cells often entered depolarization block at much lower current levels than control cells (Figure 5I,N).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5I,N.

claim: No significant differences were observed between the controls and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice for the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC).
source: We observed no significant differences between the controls and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice for the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC) or miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC), as well as the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory inputs (E/I ratio) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: No significant differences were observed between the controls and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice for the frequency and amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC).
source: We observed no significant differences between the controls and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice for the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC) or miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC), as well as the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory inputs (E/I ratio) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: No significant differences were observed between the controls and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice for the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory inputs (E/I ratio).
source: We observed no significant differences between the controls and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice for the frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC) or miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC), as well as the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory inputs (E/I ratio) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: Loss of AnkR alters the intrinsic properties of WFA+ fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons.
source: Taken together, these results show that loss of AnkR alters the intrinsic properties of WFA+ fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Kv3.1b is highly expressed in WFA+ cortical interneurons.
source: Among the Kv channels, Kv3.1b is highly expressed in WFA+ cortical interneurons (Härtig et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Härtig et al., 1999.

claim: Kv3.1b is found at some CNS nodes of Ranvier, but not AIS.
source: Kv3.1b is also found at some CNS (central nervous system) nodes of Ranvier, but not AIS (Devaux et al., 2003).

claim: AnkR is enriched in WFA+ cortical interneurons.
source: Similarly, AnkR is enriched in WFA+ cortical interneurons (Figure 2I)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: AnkR can be found at some nodes of Ranvier.
source: and can be found at some nodes of Ranvier (Ho et al., 2014), but not AIS (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ho et al., 2014 and Liu et al., 2020.

claim: AnkR is not found at AIS.
source: and can be found at some nodes of Ranvier (Ho et al., 2014), but not AIS (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2020.

source: Immunostaining of control 1- and 12-month-old somatosensory cortex showed that AnkR+ neurons were also Kv3.1b+ (Figure 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)

claim: AnkR and Kv3.1b colocalize at the neuronal membrane.
source: and that AnkR and Kv3.1b colocalize at the neuronal membrane (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: AnkR and Kv3.1b colocalize in human cortex.
source: This same colocalization was also seen in human cortex (Figure 6C).

claim: AnkR-deficient Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice have a profound reduction in Kv3.1b+ neurons at both 1- and 12 months of age.
source: Remarkably, AnkR-deficient Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice have a profound reduction in Kv3.1b+ neurons at both 1- and 12 months of age (Figure 6A,B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AnkR-deficient Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice have nearly complete loss of Kv3.1b immunofluorescence.
source: and nearly complete loss of Kv3.1b immunofluorescence (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Compared to controls, Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice have a ~50% reduction in Kv3.1b protein.
source: Compared to controls, Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice have a ~50% reduction in Kv3.1b protein (Figure 6E,F)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: The ~50% reduction in Kv3.1b protein in Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice persists in 12-month-old mice.
source: which persists in 12-month-old mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Loss of AnkR results in reduced Kv3.1a immunofluorescence at 1 month.
source: Furthermore, we also observed loss of Kv3.1a and Kv3.2, both of which may be functionally redundant and form heterotetramers with Kv3.1b; immunostaining using antibodies recognizing Kv3.1a/Kv3.1b and Kv3.2 showed a reduction in immunofluorescence at 1 month (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–G).

claim: Loss of AnkR results in reduced Kv3.2 immunofluorescence at 1 month.

evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-G.

claim: AnkR is required to maintain clustering of Kv3.1b in the somatic membrane of GABAergic interneurons.
source: These results show that AnkR is required to maintain clustering of Kv3.1b in the somatic membrane of GABAergic interneurons.

claim: AnkR-GFP efficiently co-precipitates full-length Flag-Kv3.1b.
source: AnkR-GFP efficiently co-precipitates full-length Flag-Kv3.1b (Figure 6G).

claim: AnkR-GFP binds to amino acids 1–546 of Kv3.1b.

claim: AnkR binds to the region of Kv3.1b including aa 510–546.
source: Thus, AnkR binds to the region of Kv3.1b including aa 510–546 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Amino acids 516–522 of Kv3.1b (EDCPHI) are required for AnkR binding.
source: We found that aa 516–522 of Kv3.1b (EDCPHI) are required for AnkR binding (Figure 6H).

claim: A nearly identical motif to the AnkR-binding motif in Kv3.1b is also present in Kv3.3, but not Kv3.2.

claim: Kv3.3 is highly expressed in Pv+ neurons.
source: Kv3.3 is also highly expressed in Pv+ neurons (Chang et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2007.

claim: A subset of AnkR+ neurons also express Kv3.3 in control one-month-old somatosensory cortex.
source: and immunostaining of control one-month-old somatosensory cortex showed that a subset of AnkR+ neurons also express Kv3.3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Kv3.1b co-immunoprecipitates AnkR from brain homogenates.
source: Using brain homogenates, we found that Kv3.1b co-immunoprecipitates AnkR (Figure 6J).

claim: AnkR binds directly to Kv3.1b.
source: Together, these results show that AnkR binds directly to Kv3.1b.

claim: Most peripheral nervous system nodes of Ranvier normally have high levels of Kv7.2/3 K+ channels rather than Kv3.1b.

claim: Kv7.2 K+ channel clustering requires binding to AnkG.

claim: AnkR clusters nodal Na+ channels and neurofascin 186 in the ventral roots of Ank3F/F;Chat-Cre mice.
source: AnkR clusters nodal Na+ channels (Ho et al., 2014) and neurofascin 186 in the ventral roots of Ank3F/F;Chat-Cre mice (Figure 6K).

claim: Very few nodes in ventral root normally have Kv3.1b.
source: Although very few nodes in ventral root normally have Kv3.1b (Figure 6L)
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: The replacement of AnkG by AnkR in Ank3F/F;Chat-Cre mice is sufficient to recruit and cluster Kv3.1b to nearly all nodes.
source: the replacement of AnkG by AnkR in Ank3F/F;Chat-Cre mice is sufficient to recruit and cluster Kv3.1b to nearly all nodes (Figure 6K,L)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6K,L.

claim: Nodes in control spinal cord that have high levels of AnkR also have clustered Kv3.1b.
source: and nodes in control spinal cord that have high levels of AnkR also have clustered Kv3.1b (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: AnkR recruits Kv3.3 K+ channels to nodes in AnkG-deficient ventral root axons.
source: Similarly, AnkR recruits Kv3.3 K+ channels to nodes in AnkG-deficient ventral root axons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claim: AnkG and AnkR can both cluster Na+ channels at nodes of Ranvier.
source: Together, these results show that although AnkG and AnkR can both cluster Na+ channels at nodes of Ranvier
evidence: Supported by previous studies and data in this manuscript.

claim: AnkG preferentially clusters Kv7.2/3 K+ channels and links them to the cytoskeleton through α2/β4 spectrin.
source: AnkG preferentially clusters Kv7.2/3 K+ channels and links them to the cytoskeleton through α2/β4 spectrin (Huang et al., 2017b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2017b.

claim: AnkR is both necessary and sufficient to recruit Kv3.1b/3 K+ channels to neuronal membranes and nodes of Ranvier.
source: while AnkR is both necessary and sufficient to recruit Kv3.1b/3 K+ channels to neuronal membranes and nodes of Ranvier
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: AnkR links Kv3.1b/3 K+ channels to the cytoskeleton through α2/β1 spectrin.
source: and links them to the cytoskeleton through α2/β1 spectrin (Ho et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2017a; Figure 6—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ho et al., 2014 and Huang et al., 2017a, and schematic in Figure 6—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The type of K+ channel found at nodes of Ranvier is dictated by ankyrins.
source: Thus, the type of K+ channel found at nodes of Ranvier is dictated by ankyrins.
evidence: Supported by data showing AnkG clusters Kv7.2/3 and AnkR clusters Kv3.1b/3.

claim: AnkR can substitute for AnkG to cluster Na+ channels at nodes of Ranvier.
source: Additionally, AnkR can substitute for AnkG to cluster Na+ channels at nodes of Ranvier (Ho et al., 2014) but not AIS (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ho et al., 2014 and Liu et al., 2020.

claim: AnkR cannot substitute for AnkG to cluster Na+ channels at AIS.
source: Additionally, AnkR can substitute for AnkG to cluster Na+ channels at nodes of Ranvier (Ho et al., 2014) but not AIS (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Case studies of patients with hereditary spherocytic anemia, caused by mutations in AnkR, report various neurological disturbances.
source: Intriguingly, case studies of patients with hereditary spherocytic anemia, caused by mutations in AnkR, report various neurological disturbances (Coetzer et al., 1988; McCann and Jacob, 1976; Miya et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Coetzer et al., 1988; McCann and Jacob, 1976; Miya et al., 2012.

claim: A number of recent epigenome-wide association studies in Alzheimer's disease have consistently found neuropathology-associated DNA hypermethylation of ANK1.
source: and a number of recent epigenome-wide association studies in Alzheimer's disease have consistently found neuropathology-associated DNA hypermethylation of ANK1 (ANK1 is the gene encoding AnkR) (De Jager et al., 2014; Gasparoni et al., 2018; Higham et al., 2019; Lunnon et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2019a; Smith et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Jager et al., 2014; Gasparoni et al., 2018; Higham et al., 2019; Lunnon et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2019a; Smith et al., 2019b.

claim: AnkG assembles and maintains a complex extracellular matrix (ECM) consisting of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and other ECM proteins that surround AIS and nodes of Ranvier.
source: In addition to clustering ion channels, and through its interaction with CAMs, AnkG assembles and maintains a complex extracellular matrix (ECM) consisting of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and other ECM proteins that surround AIS and nodes of Ranvier (Amor et al., 2017; Hedstrom et al., 2007; Susuki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Amor et al., 2017; Hedstrom et al., 2007; Susuki et al., 2013.

claim: The majority of PNNs surround the soma and proximal dendrites of fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive (Pv+) inhibitory interneurons.
source: The majority of PNNs surround the soma and proximal dendrites of fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive (Pv+) inhibitory interneurons and have a chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan composition similar to the perinodal and axon initial segment extracellular matrix (Fawcett et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fawcett et al., 2019.

claim: Multiple genome wide association studies (GWAS) implicate ANK1 as a schizophrenia-associated gene.
source: Multiple genome wide association studies (GWAS) implicate ANK1 as a schizophrenia-associated gene (Aberg et al., 2013; Fromer et al., 2014) Schizophrenia Working Group of the Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014
evidence: Supported by citations to Aberg et al., 2013; Fromer et al., 2014.

claim: Kv3.1b is reduced in patients with schizophrenia.
source: Kv3.1b is also reduced in patients with schizophrenia (Yanagi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yanagi et al., 2014.

claim: PNN density has been reported to be reduced in both human Alzheimer's disease brains and brains from the 5xFAD mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Similarly, PNN density has been reported to be reduced in both human Alzheimer's disease brains and brains from the 5xFAD mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (Crapser et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crapser et al., 2020.

claim: The expression of Kv3.1b in schizophrenic patients is corrected by antipsychotic drugs.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of Kv3.1b in schizophrenic patients is corrected by antipsychotic drugs (Yanagi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yanagi et al., 2014.

claim: Increased anxiety has been correlated with increased PNN density.
source: Increased anxiety has been correlated with increased PNN density (Murthy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murthy et al., 2019.

claim: The selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) fluoxetine reduces anxiety as well as PNN density.
source: Conversely, the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) fluoxetine reduces anxiety as well as PNN density (Ohira et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohira et al., 2013.

claim: Some studies have reported large reductions in PNNs throughout the brains of patients with schizophrenia.
source: Some studies have reported large reductions in PNNs throughout the brains of patients with schizophrenia (Berretta, 2012; Mauney et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berretta, 2012; Mauney et al., 2013.

claim: Mice lacking four PNN components (TnC, TnR, and the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans Bcan and neurocan) have a significant reduction in PNN structure, area, and WFA fluorescence during development, but PNNs normalize by postnatal day 35.
source: This is notable since mice lacking four PNN components (TnC, TnR, and the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans Bcan and neurocan) have a significant reduction in PNN structure, area, and WFA fluorescence during development, but PNNs normalize by postnatal day 35 (Gottschling et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gottschling et al., 2019.

claim: Loss of AnkR has more profound effects on maintenance of PNNs than even removing components of the PNNs themselves.
source: Thus, loss of AnkR has more profound effects on maintenance of PNNs than even removing components of the PNNs themselves.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with Gottschling et al., 2019 data.

claim: Both Ank1+/+;Dlx5/6-Cre and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice showed increased velocity and distance traveled compared to Ank1F/F mice in the open field test.
source: We found that all genotypes analyzed had normal locomotion, but both Ank1+/+;Dlx5/6-Cre and Ank1F/F;Dlx5/6-Cre mice showed increased velocity and distance traveled compared to Ank1F/F mice.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from open field test.

claim: The Dlx5/6-Cre transgene results in a hyperactive phenotype characterized by increased velocity and movement.
source: These results are consistent with previous reports that the Dlx5/6-Cre transgene results in a hyperactive phenotype characterized by increased velocity and movement (de Lombares et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Lombares et al., 2019.

claim: The altered excitability in AnkR-deficient neurons may reflect loss of both Kv3.1b K+ channels and reduced PNNs.
source: However, the changes in excitability may also reflect loss of both Kv3.1b K+ channels and reduced PNNs, since Bcan-deficient mice have similar changes in the excitability of their GABAergic interneurons (Favuzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Favuzzi et al., 2017 and data in this manuscript.

claim: Bcan-deficient mice have similar changes in the excitability of their GABAergic interneurons as AnkR-deficient mice.
source: However, the changes in excitability may also reflect loss of both Kv3.1b K+ channels and reduced PNNs, since Bcan-deficient mice have similar changes in the excitability of their GABAergic interneurons (Favuzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Favuzzi et al., 2017.

claim: Loss of Bcan induces changes in mPSCs.
source: however, loss of Bcan also induced changes in mPSCs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with Favuzzi et al., 2017.

claim: The AnkR-binding motif in Kv3.1b is different than the previously characterized pan ankyrin-binding motifs present in all Na+ channels.
source: This motif is different than the previously characterized pan ankyrin-binding motifs present in all Na+ channels (Garrido et al., 2003) and L1CAMs (Garver et al., 1997; Tuvia et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garrido et al., 2003; Garver et al., 1997; Tuvia et al., 1997.

claim: The AnkR-binding motif in Kv3.1b is different than the previously characterized pan ankyrin-binding motifs present in L1CAMs.
source: This motif is different than the previously characterized pan ankyrin-binding motifs present in all Na+ channels (Garrido et al., 2003) and L1CAMs (Garver et al., 1997; Tuvia et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garver et al., 1997; Tuvia et al., 1997.

claim: The Kv7.2/3 motif is highly homologous to the Na+ channel ankyrin-binding motif.
source: Although the Kv7.2/3 motif is highly homologous to the Na+ channel ankyrin-binding motif, AnkR does not cluster Kv7.2/3 (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: AnkR does not cluster Kv7.2/3.
source: Although the Kv7.2/3 motif is highly homologous to the Na+ channel ankyrin-binding motif, AnkR does not cluster Kv7.2/3 (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Kv3.3 is enriched in Pv+ interneurons in the forebrain, hippocampus, deep cerebellar nuclei, and Purkinje neurons in the cerebellum.
source: Like Kv3.1b, Kv3.3 is enriched in Pv+ interneurons in the forebrain, hippocampus, deep cerebellar nuclei, and Purkinje neurons in the cerebellum (Chang et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2007.

claim: CNS nodes with AnkR have both Kv3.1b and Kv3.3, most likely as heterotetramers.
source: Although one previous study suggested Kv3.3 is not found at nodes (Chang et al., 2007), our results show that CNS nodes with AnkR have both Kv3.1b and Kv3.3, most likely as heterotetramers.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data and citation to Chang et al., 2007.

claim: K+ channel diversity among nodes of Ranvier is dictated by the specific ankyrin scaffolds present at nodes.
source: Thus, K+ channel diversity among nodes of Ranvier is dictated by the specific ankyrin scaffolds present at nodes.
evidence: Supported by data showing AnkG clusters Kv7.2/3 and AnkR clusters Kv3.1b/3.
